title: Iain Mapa true up the eastern faces
summary: Sent into the eastern galleries of An Sloc Mòr to settle a dispute between two overseers over a cutting's bounds, the chainman Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, checks an old survey against the new digging and finds the figures will not lie flat. He walks the faces a second time before he trusts what they tell him.

title: The vein found thinning east and south
summary: A third survey of the faces gives Iain Mapa the same figures as the first two, to within an inch the chain itself can account for: the vein runs narrower to the east than the old maps show, and pinches again to the south. He sets it down in a hand that does not shake, and does not argue.

title: Iain Mapa walks the survey to Cathair dhearg
summary: Rather than trust the carters with a finding he believes the Board should see in his own hand, Iain Mapa rolls and ties his survey and walks the thirty-one miles from An Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in a day and a half, sleeping one night on the road, and tells no one at the mine beforehand what the sheet holds.

title: The Board leaves the survey unrolled
summary: Iain Mapa lays his survey before three men of Comhairle nam Mèinnean at Cathair dhearg and unties the string himself. None of the three unrolls it. He gives them the finding by mouth, plainly, and is told only, by the one in the middle, that it will be considered.

title: Ruairidh mac Ailein signs the receipt
summary: Asked for a receipt for the survey he has carried in, Iain Mapa is given four written lines naming nothing of the finding, only that a survey was received and filed. Ruairidh mac Ailein of the Board signs it, since the man in the middle will not, and Iain Mapa folds it into his pocket-book.

title: The survey filed and shown to no one
summary: Within the week Iain Mapa's survey is filed in the Board's own press at Cathair dhearg with the two years' surveys before it, and circulated to no one on the council or in any other office of the state. It lies there unread while the men who might have acted on it go on believing the mountain gives as freely as ever.

title: Iain Mapa posted to Muileann chiar
summary: Within the month Iain Mapa is told, with little explanation offered and none asked for, that he is wanted at the silver works at Muileann chiar, twenty-four miles east and a little south of An Sloc Mòr, where the Board has need of a man who holds a chain straight and asks no more than the work requires.

title: The Board's clerks move to Cathair mhòr
summary: Comhairle nam Mèinnean moves its clerks and its presses the sixteen miles from Cathair dhearg to Cathair mhòr, into leased rooms above the town's wool market, on the stated ground that a board charged with the mountain's business ought to sit nearer the mountain than it had.

title: Riaghailt a' Bhùird set down
summary: In four lines Comhairle nam Mèinnean sets down, for the first time in writing, the rule that its surveyors' work is to be kept at Cathair mhòr in the Board's own presses and not sent to Leabharlann Muileann chaol as every other office's reports are sent. No one on the council is asked to confirm it.

title: Tional nan Tuathach pays Hannah Crane's fine
summary: Word reaches Tional nan Tuathach that the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane has been fined at Baile chrom for keeping Oidhche Glaise in the open. Tional nan Tuathach votes the balance of her fine out of its own small chest without much debate, on a councillor's motion that a woman fined for standing on a beach is no threat worth agreeing with.

title: Oidhche Glaise kept indoors
summary: Forbidden the open shingle below the light, Oidhche Glaise is kept that year in a byre lent by a family who hold the old rite themselves, one night a year, in a silence the magistrate's order cannot reach any better than it reached the shore. Outsiders are still not told which night it falls on.

title: Bàta an Achaidh warped into the new harbour
summary: Of the hulls Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol cast into the fields behind Cuan dhearg two generations before, one is found sound enough to be dragged to the water, caulked and floated, and is warped into the rebuilt harbour ahead of every boat built new for it. The harbour-master keeps it moored at the quay-head as a relic rather than putting it back to work.
